question.problem: Consider the equation ${y}^{″}+y=0,$ where $y=y(t).$ If $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ is a solution, then $\lambda =$
question.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+1=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  $\lambda =\pm \text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation.
